topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Two circles, one triangle
line: Two circles swing out from each end of a segment, and the spot where they cross becomes the tip of an equilateral triangle.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Honeycomb from one segment
line: Repeating the two-circle trick from every new corner grows a whole grid of equilateral triangles that spreads across the screen.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: The collapsing compass
line: A compass that snaps shut whenever it's lifted still copies a segment to a new spot, using an equilateral triangle and two nested circles.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Triangle laid on triangle
line: One triangle lifts off, flips and lands on another with two matching sides and the angle between, and the third side clicks into place.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Flip the isosceles triangle
line: An isosceles triangle flips over like a pancake and lands exactly on itself, so its two base angles have to be the same.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: The bridge of asses
line: Both legs of an isosceles triangle stretch past the base, and two overlapping triangles light up in turn to prove the base angles match.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Why triangles don't wobble
line: Three hinged rods hold their shape while four hinged rods flop from a square into a squashed rhombus, which is why bridges use triangles.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Halving an angle
line: Compass marks land equally far out on both arms of an angle, a triangle pops up between them, and its tip splits the angle.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Fan of halves
line: An 80 degree angle gets halved again and again into 40, 20, 10 and 5 degree slices that open like a hand fan.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Cutting a segment in half
line: Two equal circles from each end cross above and below the segment, and the line through both crossings slices it exactly in half.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Equally far from both ends
line: A point slides along the perpendicular bisector while lines from it to the segment's two ends stretch together, their lengths always matching.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Dropping a plumb line
line: A circle around a point above a line cuts it twice, the midpoint of the two hits lights up, and a perpendicular drops there.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Angles on a straight line
line: A ray spins around a point on a line while two angle readouts trade degrees back and forth, always adding up to 180.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Opposite angles match
line: Two lines cross and one slowly rotates, and the angle readouts on opposite sides of the crossing change together and never disagree.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Big side, big angle
line: Drag a triangle's corner around and the longest side and biggest angle stay lit in the same color, always facing each other.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Sticks that can't close
line: Sticks of 2 and 3 swing up from a base of 6 and can't meet; shrink the base to 4 and they connect.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: The detour is always longer
line: A point wanders off the straight path from A to B, and a counter shows the bent route through it is always longer.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Pinch inside the triangle
line: A point inside a triangle pulls two lines in from the base corners; their total length shrinks while the angle between them grows.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Triangle from three lengths
line: Circles of radius 4 and 5 grow from the ends of a 6-long base and cross at the third corner; stretch it, they miss.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Opening the hinge
line: Two hinged sticks of fixed length open like scissors, and the third side between their tips grows on screen as the angle widens.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Two angles pin a triangle
line: Rays fire from both ends of a fixed base at 50 and 70 degrees and can cross at only one point, locking the triangle.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Parallel lines and a transversal
line: A slanted line tilts across two parallel lines, and the eight angles it makes split into two color groups that change in sync.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Sliding an angle down
line: The angle at the top crossing slides down the transversal to the bottom parallel line and fits perfectly over the angle already there.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Tear off the corners
line: The three corners of a paper triangle snip off and slide together, fitting side by side into a perfectly straight 180 degree line.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Parallel line through the top
line: A line parallel to the base appears through the top corner, and both base angles slide up to sit beside the top angle.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Walk around a triangle
line: An arrow walks around a triangle, turning at each corner, and its three turns add up to exactly one full 360 degree spin.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Angles of any polygon
line: Diagonals from one corner cut a pentagon into 3 triangles and a hexagon into 4, so the angle total grows 180 per side.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Two halves of a parallelogram
line: A diagonal splits a parallelogram, and one half spins 180 degrees around the center to land exactly on the other half.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Leaning parallelogram
line: A parallelogram's top edge slides along its parallel line, so the shape leans further and further while its area counter stays at 24.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Cut and slide
line: A triangle cut from one end of a rectangle slides to the other end, making a parallelogram with the same base, height and area.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Deck of cards triangle
line: A triangle sliced into 12 thin strips gets pushed sideways like a deck of cards, its tip sliding while its area holds still.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Triangle is half a parallelogram
line: A triangle's rotated twin clicks onto it to form a parallelogram on the same base, so the triangle is exactly half its area.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Two rectangles that always match
line: A point slides along a rectangle's diagonal, cutting it into four pieces, and the two pieces off the diagonal reshape but keep equal areas.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Same area, new base
line: A 2 by 6 rectangle uses the diagonal trick to become a 3 by 4 rectangle on a new base, area still 12.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Any shape into a rectangle
line: A lumpy pentagon is cut into triangles, each becomes a strip of the same width, and the strips stack into one equal-area rectangle.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Pythagoras by rearranging
line: Four 3-4-5 triangles slide around inside a 7 by 7 square, and the tilted 25 square becomes a 9 square plus a 16 square.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Euclid's windmill
line: The squares on the legs shear into parallelograms, rotate, and shear again into two rectangles that exactly fill the square on the hypotenuse.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Perigal's puzzle pieces
line: The 16 square on the longer leg is cut into four pieces, and they wrap around the 9 square to fill the 25 square.

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: Tilted squares on a dot grid
line: On a dot grid, a tilted square's area comes from a bigger square minus four corner triangles, and it always equals a² + b².

topic: Book I: Triangles, parallels and area
title: The rope stretcher's right angle
line: A loop of rope with 12 evenly spaced knots is pulled tight into a 3-4-5 triangle, and the corner snaps to exactly 90 degrees.

title: Splitting a long rectangle
line: A 3 by 7 rectangle splits into 3 by 2, 3 by 4 and 3 by 1 pieces, showing 3(2+4+1) = 6+12+3.

title: Square of a sum
line: A 5 by 5 square cut at 3 + 2 flies apart into tiles of 9, 6, 6 and 4: a², ab, ab, b².

title: The forgotten middle
line: Squares of 3 and 2 drop into a 5 by 5 square, leaving two 3 by 2 gaps that flash red.

title: Difference of squares by sliding
line: A small square is cut from a big square's corner, and the leftover L-shape rearranges into a rectangle: a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b).

title: Squarest rectangle wins
line: A rectangle with perimeter 20 morphs from 9 by 1 toward 5 by 5, and its area counter climbs to a peak of 25.

title: Completing the square
line: A 6 by x strip beside an x² square splits in half, hugs two sides, and a 3 by 3 corner completes the square.

title: Solving a quadratic with tiles
line: Tiles for x² + 6x total 16, a 9 corner makes a 5 by 5 square, so x + 3 = 5.

title: Square of a difference
line: Two a by b strips are cut from an a² square, the twice-removed b² corner is added back, and (a − b)² remains.

title: Four rectangles around a hole
line: Four 3 by 1 rectangles pinwheel around a 2 by 2 hole to build a 4 by 4 square: 4·3 + 4 = 16.

title: Two squares, average and gap
line: Squares of side 5 and 1 rearrange into two copies each of a 3 square and a 2 square, both totaling 26.

title: Hunting the golden cut
line: A point slides along a segment of length 1 until the square on the long piece equals the whole-times-short rectangle, at 0.618.

title: Euclid's golden construction
line: A line from the middle of a square's side to a far corner swings down like a compass arm onto the golden cut.

title: Obtuse triangles overshoot
line: As a triangle's corner opens past 90 degrees, the big square outgrows the two small squares by two thin rectangles that keep getting bigger.

title: Bigger angle, bigger square
line: A triangle's angle sweeps from 30 to 150 degrees while a bar shows c² − (a² + b²), crossing zero exactly at 90.

title: Squaring a rectangle with a semicircle
line: A 4 by 9 rectangle unrolls into a 13-long diameter, a semicircle rises, and the height at the joint is 6: a 36 square.

title: Finding a lost center
line: A chord is drawn, its perpendicular bisector crosses the circle as a diameter, and halving that diameter lights up the hidden center point.

title: The center splits every chord
line: A chord slides up and down a circle while the perpendicular from the center always lands on its midpoint, both halves reading equal.

title: Longest and shortest reach
line: From a point inside a circle, a line spins to the edge, and its length graph peaks through the center and dips opposite.

title: Two circles, at most two crossings
line: One circle glides across another while an intersection counter reads 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, and it never manages to reach 3.

title: Spinning a fixed chord
line: A chord of fixed length rotates around inside a circle at a constant distance from the center, and its midpoint traces a smaller circle.

title: Diameter is the longest chord
line: A chord slides from the edge of a circle toward the center, its length counting up and topping out as a diameter.

title: Secant becomes tangent
line: A line through a point on a circle rotates until both crossings merge, and right then it sits at 90 degrees to the radius.

title: Tangent from an outside point
line: A bigger circle through an outside point, a perpendicular and one more line pin down exactly where the tangent from it touches.

title: Half the center angle
line: A point slides around a circle above a fixed chord, its angle reading 35 degrees while the center's angle on that arc reads 70.

title: Two isosceles triangles
line: A diameter through the edge point splits the picture into two isosceles triangles, whose outer angles double to explain the factor of two.

title: Same view from every seat
line: Spectators placed anywhere along an arc behind a goal all see the two posts at the same 40 degree angle, their angle readouts frozen.

title: Opposite corners add to 180
line: Four points slide around a circle and the quadrilateral's angles change wildly, but each pair of opposite corners always adds up to 180.

title: Rebuilding a broken plate
line: Two chords on a broken arc get perpendicular bisectors that cross at the center, and the rest of the circle sweeps back into place.

title: Square corners in a semicircle
line: A point slides along a semicircle above a diameter, and the angle it makes with the diameter's ends reads 90 degrees every time.

title: Inside, on and outside
line: A point drags around a diameter: its angle reads over 90 inside the circle, exactly 90 on it, and under 90 outside.

title: A rectangle hidden in a circle
line: A right triangle in a semicircle spins half a turn about the center into a rectangle whose two diagonals are both diameters.

title: Tangent and chord angle
line: A point on the circle slides into the tangent point, and its inscribed angle morphs into the chord-tangent angle without changing size.

title: Crossing chords keep their product
line: One chord rotates around where it crosses another, and both products of their pieces, like 3 × 8 and 4 × 6, stay 24.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Growing the incircle
line: Three angle bisectors meet at one point, and a circle inflates from there until it kisses all three sides of the triangle at once.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: The circle through three corners
line: Perpendicular bisectors meet at a center, a circle passes through all three corners, and dragging one corner past 90 degrees pushes the center outside.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Squares and circles forever
line: A square inscribes in a circle, a circle inscribes in that square, and the pattern keeps nesting inward as the view zooms in forever.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: The triangle that contains itself
line: Bisecting a base angle of a 36-72-72 triangle cuts off a smaller copy of itself, and repeating spirals into tinier copies.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Building the golden triangle
line: A line cut at the golden point plus one circle produce a triangle whose base angles light up as exactly double the top angle.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Pentagon from a golden triangle
line: A 36-72-72 triangle sits in a circle, and bisecting its base angles hits the circle at the last two corners of a pentagon.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Star inside a pentagon
line: A pentagon's diagonals draw a five-point star, the star's center holds a smaller upside-down pentagon, and the pattern repeats inward.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Pentagon hugging a circle
line: Tangent lines at the five corners of an inscribed pentagon stretch out until they meet, forming a bigger pentagon wrapped snugly around the circle.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Six steps around the circle
line: A compass opened to the radius steps around a circle and lands back at its start after exactly six steps, marking a regular hexagon.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Six triangles make a hexagon
line: Six equilateral triangles fan out from the center, each with a 60 degree point, and together they fill 360 degrees into a hexagon.

topic: Book IV: Polygons in and around circles
title: Fifteen from three and five
line: A triangle and pentagon share a top corner in a circle, and the tiny gap between their nearest corners steps around 15 times.

title: Three bars, tripled two ways
line: Three colored bars are each copied three times, then the nine copies shuffle into three identical stacks of all three bars.

title: Two rulers that keep in step
line: Ticks at multiples of 3 and 5 on one ruler, and of 6 and 10 on another, interleave in the same order.

title: Same-shape rectangles add up
line: Rectangles 2×3, 4×6 and 6×9 snap together corner to corner along one diagonal, making a 12×18 rectangle of the same shape.

title: The outside pair always wins
line: Bars of 9, 6, 6 and 4 are in proportion; laid end to end, 9 plus 4 outruns 6 plus 6.

title: Sliding the apex
line: A triangle's top corner glides parallel to its base while its area stays frozen, then the base stretches and the area follows.

title: Five slices, five equal areas
line: A triangle's base is cut into five equal pieces, and the five thin triangles to the apex shear into identical copies.

title: The parallel cut
line: A line parallel to the base slides up a triangle, and the ratio readouts on the two sides change together, always equal.

title: Finding parallel by ratio
line: A point is dragged along a triangle's side; the cutting line turns green the moment both sides split in the same ratio.

title: Where the bisector lands
line: The angle between sides 6 and 4 is split in half, and the bisector cuts the base into pieces 3 and 2.

title: Euclid's trick for the bisector
line: One side extends and a parallel line closes an isosceles triangle, turning the bisector question into a plain parallel-line cut.

title: Measuring a pyramid with a stick
line: A 1 m stick casts a 2 m shadow beside a pyramid's 70 m shadow; the sun triangles match, giving height 35.

title: Same angles, scaled sides
line: A 3-4-5 triangle slides into the corner of a 6-8-10 triangle with matching angles, and every side pair shows ratio 2.

title: Three triangles, one shape
line: An altitude from the right angle splits a 3-4-5 triangle, and both pieces spin and scale until they sit on the whole.

title: Pythagoras from similar pieces
line: The two triangles inside a 3-4-5 triangle have areas in ratio 9 : 16 : 25 with the whole, so they add up.

title: Cutting a stick in five, no ruler
line: Five equal steps go along a slanted ray, the last joins the segment's end, and parallel lines slide over to cut fifths.

title: A zigzag that multiplies
line: Lines bounce between two rays, each parallel to the last, marking lengths 2, 3, 4.5, 6.75 that grow by 1.5 each time.

title: Multiplying with parallel lines
line: 1 and 3 on one ray, 2 on the other: sliding the 1-to-2 line over to 3 lands it on 6.

title: The square root machine
line: A semicircle stands on segments 1 and x; as x counts up to 9, the height above the joint reads its square root.

title: Never taller than the radius
line: A split point slides along a semicircle's diameter; the height above it stays under the radius, touching it only at the middle.

title: Rectangles of area 12
line: A rectangle squashes from 1×12 through 2×6, 3×4 and 6×2, area fixed, while its corner traces the curve xy = 12.

title: Cross-multiplying with rectangles
line: 2/3 and 4/6 swap partners into 2×6 and 3×4 rectangles that match; 2/3 against 3/4 gives 8 against 9.

title: A rectangle that becomes a square
line: A 2×8 rectangle is cut in half and the halves stack into a 4×4 square, the middle term between 2 and 8.

title: Rebuilding a pentagon on a new base
line: A pentagon fans into three triangles from one corner, and each is copied with the same angles onto a longer base.

title: Double the side, four copies
line: A triangle with doubled sides splits into four copies of the original, with tripled sides into nine.

title: The scale slider
line: A triangle's scale factor slides from 1 to 3 while side and area readouts climb, and the area values draw a parabola.

title: Every piece grows the same
line: A pentagon and its 2× twin split into triangles from one corner, and each small triangle fits four times into its partner.

title: Stretch one way, then the other
line: A 2×3 rectangle stretches sideways to 4×3, doubling its area, then up to 4×5; the two growth factors multiply.

title: Riding the diagonal
line: A point slides along a parallelogram's diagonal, and the two small parallelograms it carves out keep the big one's shape.

title: Same shape, new size
line: A star-shaped polygon grows until its area matches a 3×5 rectangle, and the scale factor it needs is a square root.

title: The biggest rectangle on a fence
line: A rectangle with sides x and 10 minus x slides along a 10-unit base; its area peaks at 25 as a square.

title: Solving x(10 − x) = 21 by cutting
line: A 2×2 square is cut from a 5×5 square's corner, and the L-shaped rest slides into a 3×7 rectangle: x = 3.

title: Finding the golden cut
line: A cut point slides along a segment; readouts for whole-to-big and big-to-small ratios chase each other until both read 1.618.

title: The golden rectangle spiral
line: A square is cut from a golden rectangle, leaving a smaller golden rectangle, again and again, and quarter circles trace a spiral.

title: Euclid's compass recipe
line: A square is drawn on the segment, an arc swings from one side's midpoint, and where it lands is the golden cut.

title: Fibonacci closing in
line: Bars of 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 grow, and each bar's ratio to the last bounces around 1.618, closing in.

title: Pythagoras with semicircles
line: Semicircles on a 3-4-5 triangle's sides fill with colored liquid, and the two small ones pour exactly into the big one.

title: The triangle is its own proof
line: A right triangle splits along its altitude into two similar copies on the legs, which together make the copy on the hypotenuse.

title: Hippocrates' moons
line: The hypotenuse semicircle folds over the triangle, and the two crescents left on the legs have exactly the triangle's area.

title: Peeling the arc off
line: A central angle sweeps from 30° to 90°, and the arc it cuts peels off and lays flat, growing in step.

title: Subtract until one is left
line: Bars of 21 and 8 chop each other down to 5, 3, 2, then 1; a lone unit means no common measure.

title: Squares in a 13 by 8 rectangle
line: The biggest possible squares are cut from a 13×8 rectangle: sizes 8, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1, Fibonacci all the way down.

title: The common ruler for 48 and 18
line: Bars of 48 and 18 subtract back and forth until 6 is left, then a 6-long ruler hops evenly along both bars.

title: Tiling with the biggest squares
line: An 18×48 rectangle loses two 18×18 squares, then a 12×12, and two 6×6 squares finish it exactly.

title: Chopping 15 to see 6
line: Bars of 15 and 6 are both cut into 3-long pieces, showing 6 is two of five pieces, or 2/5 of 15.

title: Turning 3 times 5 sideways
line: A 3-by-5 grid of 15 dots rotates a quarter turn into 5 rows of 3, so multiplying order can't matter.

title: Why primes can't be split
line: 6 divides 4×9 by splitting into 2 and 3 across the factors; prime 5 can't split, so it must divide one whole.

title: Every number hides a prime
line: 84 breaks into 2×42, then 2×21, then 3×7; the pieces keep shrinking, so the chain must hit a prime.

title: Shrinking 24 : 36 : 60
line: Bars of 24, 36 and 60 are cut into 12-long pieces, and counting pieces gives the smallest version, 2 : 3 : 5.

title: Two frogs on a number line
line: One frog hops 4 at a time, another hops 6; their landing spots light up, and the first shared spot is 12.

title: Gears coming back around
line: Gears with 12 and 18 teeth spin with one marked tooth each, and the marks meet again after 36 teeth pass.

title: Shared spots come every 12
line: Frogs hopping 4 and 6 run on to 60, and every spot both hit is a multiple of 12.

title: Three blinking lights
line: Lights blinking every 3, 4 and 6 seconds flash along a timeline, and all three first fire together at 12.

title: A chocolate bar for everyone
line: The smallest chocolate bar that splits evenly into halves, thirds and quarters builds up square by square: exactly 12 pieces.

topic: Book VIII: Numbers in continued proportion
title: A chain where nothing divides
line: In 16, 24, 36, 54, 81 each step multiplies by 3/2, and every try at dividing one term by another fails.

topic: Book VIII: Numbers in continued proportion
title: The rectangle between two squares
line: A 2×2 square stretches one side into a 2×3 rectangle, then the other into 3×3: 4, 6, 9, each times 3/2.

topic: Book VIII: Numbers in continued proportion
title: Swapping factors from 8 to 27
line: Chips reading 2·2·2 swap a 2 for a 3 one at a time, giving 8, 12, 18, 27, each step times 3/2.

topic: Book VIII: Numbers in continued proportion
title: Tiling a square with squares
line: A 6×6 grid tiles perfectly with 2×2 squares because 2 divides 6, but 4×4 tiles leave gaps.

title: Squares and cubes among the doublings
line: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 light up: every second is a square, every third a cube, and 64 is both.

title: The only divisors of 32
line: Every number from 1 to 32 tries to divide 32, failures fade, and only 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 survive.

title: Two trees, same leaves
line: 360 is factored two different ways with factor trees, and both sets of leaves sort into 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5.

title: Always one left over
line: 2×3×5 + 1 = 31 is measured with rulers of 2, 3 and 5, and each one ends exactly one unit short.

title: The 30031 surprise
line: 2×3×5×7×11×13 + 1 = 30031 isn't prime, but it splits into 59 × 509, two primes missing from the list.

title: A machine that makes new primes
line: Multiply the primes so far, add 1, keep its smallest prime factor, repeat: 2, 3, 7, 43, 13, 53 appear.

title: Odd numbers pair up
line: Odd numbers drawn as dot pairs plus one loose dot merge, and with an even count the loose dots pair off perfectly.

title: Odd times odd leaves a dot
line: Dominoes tile a 5×7 grid of dots row by row, and however they shift, one dot stays uncovered.

title: The halving machine
line: 64 is halved over and over, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, never hitting an odd number, while 24 stalls at 3.

title: Sum of 1, 3, 9, 27
line: Bars 1, 3, 9 and 27 stack beside the next bar, 81; cut 1 off it and the rest splits into two 40s.

title: Halves filling a square
line: A square fills with 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and the empty corner always equals the last piece added.

title: 28 is perfect
line: 1+2+4 = 7 is prime, so 4×7 = 28, and its divisor bars 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 stack to exactly 28.

title: Hunting perfect numbers
line: Doubling sums 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127 are tested; each prime makes 6, 28, 496, 8128, while 15 and 63 fail.

title: Two rows of divisors
line: Divisors of 496 line up in two rows, 1 to 16 and 31 to 248, summing to 31 and 465: 496 exactly.

title: Halving past any target
line: A bar of length 1 keeps halving beside a tiny 0.01 rod, and a counter shows it slips below after 7 cuts.

title: More than half, or not enough
line: Two bars of length 2: one loses over half of what's left and vanishes; the other loses 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and stalls above 1.

title: The square's diagonal never stops
line: Subtract a square's side from its diagonal; the leftovers form a smaller square and diagonal, so the subtraction repeats forever, zooming in.

title: One race ends, one doesn't
line: Rods 7 and 5 subtract down to a common unit in four steps, while a square's side and diagonal keep subtracting forever.

title: Rods that find their common unit
line: Rods of 21 and 15 chop each other in turn: 21 leaves 6, 15 leaves 3, and 3 fits 6 exactly.

title: Shrinking the ruler to fit
line: A ruler's ticks shrink until rods of 1.5 and 2.5 both end exactly on a tick, at spacing 0.5: ratio 3 to 5.

title: Squares on rods, square numbers
line: Rods of 2 and 3 grow squares of 4 and 9 tiles; a side and diagonal grow areas 1 and 2, and 2 isn't square.

title: Rectangle that falls short by a square
line: A point slides along a line of 10; the rectangle x by (10 − x) reshapes as its area traces a parabola peaking at 25.

title: An L of dots that's a square
line: An L of 9 dots wraps a 4 by 4 grid into a 5 by 5 square; 9 is square, so 3, 4, 5 appears.

title: Folding a rectangle around a square
line: An 8 by 2 rectangle of tiles splits and folds around a 3 by 3 square into a 5 by 5: 16 + 9 = 25.

topic: Book XII: Areas and volumes by exhaustion
title: Polygons grow with diameter squared
line: A lopsided pentagon in a circle scales as the diameter goes 1, 2, 3, and its area counter reads 1, 4, 9.

topic: Book XII: Areas and volumes by exhaustion
title: Doubling sides toward the circle
line: A square in a unit circle doubles to 8, 16, 32, 64 sides while its area counter climbs from 2.00 toward 3.14.

topic: Book XII: Areas and volumes by exhaustion
title: Two circles, one ratio
line: Circles of diameter 2 and 3 get matching polygons with ever more sides; the area ratio counter stays locked at 4/9.

topic: Book XII: Areas and volumes by exhaustion
title: Each sliver loses over half
line: Zoom into one sliver between a circle and a square; the triangle that fills it on doubling always covers more than half.

topic: Book XII: Areas and volumes by exhaustion
title: Polygon squeezed between two circles
line: A square, octagon, 16-gon, then 32-gon fill a circle of radius 1 until one finally clears an inner circle of radius 0.9.

title: Five squares make one
line: Five unit squares in a plus sign are cut and slid into one square, whose side is a golden cut's long piece plus 1.

title: Two squares fill three
line: Squares on a golden-cut line and on its short piece pour their area into three squares on the long piece, filling them exactly.

title: A golden line keeps growing
line: A golden-cut line gains its long piece again and again, growing 1, 1.618, 2.618, 4.236, while its ratio counter never budges.

title: Locking a floppy pentagon
line: A pentagon of five equal hinged sticks wobbles through lopsided shapes until three angles match, then snaps into the regular pentagon.

title: Diagonals cut in golden ratio

line: Numbers 1, 2, 3 drop into a box labeled f(x)=2x+3, come out as 5, 7, 9, and fly to their spots on a graph.

source_title: Purplemath: What are relations? What are functions (in math)?
title: Vertical line sweep
line: A vertical line sweeps across y=x² hitting it once each time, then across x=y² where it hits twice and flashes red.

source_title: Purplemath: What are relations? What are functions (in math)?
title: Arrows from inputs
line: An arrow diagram links inputs to outputs; when one input sprouts a second arrow, the relation stops being a function.

title: Adding k lifts the graph
line: As k counts from −3 to 3, y=x²+k rides up and down the plane without changing shape.

title: Why minus moves right
line: For y=(x−3)², each table row's point slides 3 to the right, because the input now has to be 3 bigger to give the same output.

title: Steering a square root
line: y=√x moves step by step to y=√(x+2)−1 while its starting point leaves a trail from (0,0) to (−2,−1).

source_title: Purplemath: How do you graph quadratic functions / parabolas?
title: The 1-3-5 staircase
line: From the vertex of y=x², steps of over 1 and up 1, 3, 5 build both arms; for y=2x² the steps become 2, 6, 10.

source_title: Purplemath: Systems of Linear Inequalities: Solving by Graphing
title: Where the shadings overlap
line: y≥x−2, y<−2x+4 and x≥0 each shade a half-plane in a different color until only the triangle where all three overlap stays lit.

title: Arms reaching from 3
line: For |x−3|<2, arms of length 2 reach out from 3 and light up 1 to 5; flip to > and two outer rays light instead.

source_title: Purplemath: How do you solve quadratic inequalities? (steps)
title: Above the axis wins
line: The parabola y=x²−x−6 crosses at −2 and 3, the parts above the axis glow and drop onto a number line as two rays.

source_title: Purplemath: What is linear programming? What is it used for?
title: Sliding the profit line
line: Over a polygon of feasible points, the line 3x+2y=P slides outward until it touches only one corner, the best answer.

source_title: Purplemath: What is linear programming? What is it used for?
title: Why corners win
line: A dot walks along an edge of the feasible region while P=3x+2y counts steadily up, so the best value must sit at an endpoint.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the numerical approximation of zeroes?
title: Halving toward a root
line: x³−x−1 changes sign between 1 and 2; the interval halves again and again while the camera zooms and digits of 1.3247 lock in.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the 4 function operations? (w/ examples)
title: Stacking graphs to add
line: Vertical sticks from the axis up to y=x² and y=x stack end to end, and their tops trace out the graph of y=x²+x.

source_title: Purplemath: Graphing polynomials, radicals, piecewise, etc.
title: Piecewise in pieces
line: Three formulas draw faintly across the whole plane, then each gets trimmed to its own interval with open and closed dots at the seams.

title: Zoom out to the ends
line: y=x³−4x²+x+6 wiggles near the origin, but as the camera zooms out it becomes nearly identical to plain y=x³.

title: Four ways the arms point
line: Flipping the leading sign and switching between even and odd degree swings a polynomial's two end arrows into all four up/down patterns.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Rational Roots Test? How does it work?
title: The fraction factory
line: Factors of 6 and of 2 pair up into every fraction p/q, duplicates merge, and the list settles onto a number line of candidate roots.

title: Remainder equals height
line: Dividing x³−2x+5 by x−2 leaves remainder 9, and on the graph the point above x=2 rises to height 9 as well.

title: Formula meets the crossings
line: For y=x²−2x−3, −b/2a marks the axis of symmetry, then ±√(b²−4ac)/2a steps 2 each way and lands on −1 and 3.

title: The discriminant decides
line: As c rises in x²+2x+c the parabola lifts, the discriminant 4−4c counts down through zero, and crossings go from 2 to 1 to 0.

title: Coefficients into slots
line: The colored a, b, c of 2x²+3x−5 fly into matching slots of the formula and simplify to 1 and −5/2.

source_title: Purplemath: Completing the Square: Deriving the Quadratic Formula
title: Deriving the formula with a square
line: ax²+bx+c=0 divides by a, the x-square grows two b/2a strips, the missing corner fills, and the steps morph into the quadratic formula.

source_title: Purplemath: Completing the Square: Deriving the Quadratic Formula
title: Roots from the vertex
line: A parabola written as a(x−h)²+k crosses at h±√(−k/a); swapping in h and k from b and c turns that into the formula.

source_title: Purplemath: Sequences and Series: Terminology and Notation
title: Sigma as a counter
line: As i ticks from 1 to 5 in the sum of 2i−1, each term pops out as an L of dots, nesting into a 5×5 square.

source_title: Purplemath: Solving quadratics by solving their factors
title: Either factor can be zero
line: Lines y=x−2 and y=x+5 multiply into a parabola, and wherever either line hits zero the parabola hits zero too.

source_title: Purplemath: What are systems of non-linear equations?
title: Line meets circle
line: The line y=x+k slides across the circle x²+y²=25, and the intersection count drops from 2 to 1 at tangency to 0.

source_title: Purplemath: Special Factoring: Differences of Squares
title: Cutting a square from a square
line: A small b-square is cut from an a-square, the L-shape's strip swings around, and it becomes an (a+b) by (a−b) rectangle.

title: Flipping over the x-axis
line: Each point (a, b) of the sideways parabola x=y²−4 walks straight across the x-axis to (a, −b) and lands back on the curve.

source_title: Purplemath: How does synthetic division of polynomials work?
title: Bring down, multiply, add
line: Dividing x³+2x²−5x−6 by x+3, coefficients drop, multiply by −3, and add down the row until the remainder 0 glows.

title: Double x, see what y does
line: x doubles on both y=2x and y=12/x; on the line y doubles, on the hyperbola y halves, shown by growing and shrinking bars.

source_title: Purplemath: What are vertical asymptotes (of rtnl functions)?
title: Racing toward x=2
line: A dot on y=1/(x−2) creeps toward x=2 from both sides while its y readout dives toward −∞ and shoots toward +∞.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Binomial Theorem?
title: (a+b)² as an area
line: An (a+b)-sided square splits into a², two ab rectangles and b², and the 1, 2, 1 coefficients appear as the pieces are counted.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Binomial Theorem?
title: Pascal feeds the expansion
line: Pascal's triangle builds by adding pairs, then row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 drops into (a+b)⁴ as a's powers fall and b's rise.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Binomial Theorem?
title: Picking a or b four times
line: All 16 ways to pick a or b from four brackets, like abab, sort into piles of sizes 1, 4, 6, 4, 1.

title: Unstacking a fraction
line: Top and bottom of a stacked fraction get multiplied by the common denominator 6x, and the little denominators cancel away visibly.

source_title: Purplemath: What the Heck are Imaginary Numbers?
title: Powers of i go around
line: Multiplying by i turns a point a quarter turn each time, carrying it from 1 to i to −1 to −i and back to 1.

source_title: Purplemath: What the Heck are Imaginary Numbers?
title: Adding complex numbers as arrows
line: 3+2i and 1−4i become arrows on the plane, tip meets tail, and the sum 4−2i is where the second arrow ends.

source_title: Purplemath: Function Composition Using Only Sets of Points
title: Through two machines
line: x=1 follows arrows through the point set g to 3, then through f to 7; another input gets stuck where f has no match.

title: Slicing the cone
line: In a side view of a double cone, a cutting line tilts and the slice beside it turns from circle to ellipse to parabola to hyperbola.

title: Which conic from the signs
line: Sliders change A and C in Ax²+Cy²=1, and the graph morphs from circle to ellipse to hyperbola as their signs and sizes change.

source_title: Purplemath: What are parabolas, their equations, their rules?
title: Same distance to both
line: A point moves so its distance to the focus (0,1) and to the line y=−1 always match, and its trail draws a parabola.

source_title: Purplemath: What are parabolas, their equations, their rules?
title: Dish to focus
line: Vertical rays fall into a parabola, bounce off its wall, and every one of them passes through the focus.

source_title: Purplemath: Circles in algebra: what to know and what to do
title: Pythagoras draws a circle
line: A point circles (2,1) at distance 5 while its right triangle's legs x−2 and y−1 change length and their squares always sum to 25.

source_title: Purplemath: What are ellipses? What are their vocabulary words?
title: String and two pins
line: A pencil point moves with distances to foci (±3,0) changing, but their sum stays 10, tracing out an ellipse.

source_title: Purplemath: What are ellipses? What are their vocabulary words?
title: Whispering gallery
line: Rays leave one focus of an ellipse in every direction, bounce off the curve, and all meet at the other focus.

source_title: Purplemath: Hyperbolas: Their Equations, Graphs, and Terms
title: Constant difference
line: A point keeps its distances to foci (±5,0) differing by exactly 6, and both branches of a hyperbola appear as it moves.

source_title: Purplemath: Hyperbolas: Their Equations, Graphs, and Terms
title: Hugging the asymptotes
line: For x²/9−y²/16=1, a 6-by-8 box's diagonals extend into asymptotes, and as the camera zooms out the branches cling to them.

source_title: Purplemath: What is Cramer's Rule, and how does it work?
title: Cramer's rule as areas
line: The column vectors of a 2×2 system form a parallelogram; swapping one column for the answer column makes another, and x is their area ratio.

source_title: Purplemath: What is a determinant? How do I work with one?
title: Determinant as area
line: Columns (3,1) and (1,2) span a parallelogram of area 5; as one column turns parallel to the other, the area shrinks to 0.

source_title: Purplemath: What is a determinant? How do I work with one?
title: Criss-cross diagonals
line: Arrows draw down one diagonal of a 2×2 and up the other, then a 3×3 copies its first two columns for six diagonal products.

title: Adding versus doubling
line: Two bars grow side by side, one adding 2 each step and one doubling from 1, until the doubling bar shoots off screen.

title: Doubling every five steps
line: On y=3·2^(x/5), every 5 units right the height doubles, from 3 to 6 to 12 to 24, marked by bracket after bracket.

source_title: Purplemath: The graphical properties of exponential functions
title: Turning the base dial
line: As b slides from 0.5 to 3 in y=b^x, the curve pivots through (0,1), going flat at b=1 and flipping from decay to growth.

source_title: Purplemath: How do you graph logs without a calculator?
title: Swapping exponents into logs
line: Points like (3,8) on y=2^x swap to (8,3), crossing the line y=x, and together draw y=log₂x.

source_title: Purplemath: How do you graph logs without a calculator?
title: Doubling to climb one
line: On y=log₂x, marks at x=1, 2, 4, 8, 16 rise by exactly one each, so each equal step up needs twice the distance right.

source_title: Purplemath: Graphing rational functions without a calculator
title: Sketching from clues
line: For y=(x+1)/(x−2), intercepts appear as dots, asymptotes x=2 and y=1 dash in, test points land, and two curve pieces get drawn.

source_title: Purplemath: What is "proof by induction"? How does it work?
title: Adding one more column
line: A staircase of k(k+1)/2 dots gains a column of k+1 dots, and the formula morphs into (k+1)(k+2)/2 to match.

source_title: Purplemath: What is "proof by induction"? How does it work?
title: Dominoes that must fall
line: A first domino labeled n=1 falls, and each domino k is shown knocking over k+1, so the whole endless row goes down.

source_title: Purplemath: Simple methods for solving polynomial inequalities
title: Sign chart from factors
line: (x+2), (x−1) and (x−4) each get a sign row that flips at its zero, the product row fills in, and the graph above confirms it.

source_title: Purplemath: How to solve rational inequalities, step-by-step
title: Holes and zeros split the line
line: For (x−3)/(x+1)≤0, the line splits at an open hole at −1 and a closed dot at 3, and test points light up the middle interval.

source_title: Purplemath: Inverse relations and how to find them
title: Swapping across y=x
line: Points (1,2), (2,4), (3,4) swap their coordinates and fly across y=x; two land above x=4, so the inverse fails the vertical line test.

source_title: Purplemath: What are logarithms, and why are they so hard?
title: Log counts the multiplying
line: For log₂32, 2 multiplies by itself while a counter ticks 1 to 5 until it reaches 32, so the log is the count.

source_title: Purplemath: What are logarithms, and why are they so hard?
title: Stretching a ruler into a log scale
line: Points 1, 10, 100, 1000 slide from an ordinary number line to equal spacing, each step meaning one more power of ten.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the rules for rearranging logarithms?
title: A slide rule multiplies
line: Two log-scale rulers slide so 1 sits over 2, and 6 appears under 3, because adding lengths log 2 and log 3 makes log 6.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the rules for rearranging logarithms?
title: Change of base is a stretch
line: The graph of log₁₀x stretches vertically by about 3.32 and lands exactly on log₂x.

source_title: Purplemath: Matrix basics: what they are and what's their lingo
title: From system to grid
line: In a system of three equations, the variables and plus signs fade, and the coefficients slide together into a bracketed grid.

source_title: Purplemath: How to add one matrix to another? Entry-wise!
title: Adding moves a triangle
line: A triangle's vertex coordinates sit in a matrix; adding a matrix of 2s and 1s shifts every vertex, and the triangle slides together.

source_title: Purplemath: What's a scalar? What is matrix multiplication?
title: Row meets column
line: A row slides across a column, matching entries multiply and pop out, and their sum drops into one spot of the product.

source_title: Purplemath: What's a scalar? What is matrix multiplication?
title: A matrix bends the plane
line: A grid shears under the matrix [[1,1],[0,1]]; the arrows for x and y land on the matrix's columns while grid lines stay parallel.

source_title: Purplemath: What's a scalar? What is matrix multiplication?
title: Scalars stretch the shape
line: Multiplying a triangle's coordinate matrix by 3 pushes every vertex three times farther from the origin.

source_title: Purplemath: What's a scalar? What is matrix multiplication?
title: Order matters
line: A square is rotated then sheared, and a copy is sheared then rotated; the two end up as different shapes, so AB≠BA.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the three matrix row operations?
title: Row moves, same answer
line: Each row operation on a 2×2 system redraws its two lines: scaling leaves a line alone, adding rows swings one line around the fixed intersection.

source_title: Purplemath: What is an inverse matrix, and what's it used for?
title: Undoing a matrix
line: A square turns into a parallelogram under [[2,1],[1,1]], then its inverse matrix pulls it back to the exact same square.

source_title: Purplemath: What are minors and cofactors? What are they for?
title: Cross out and shrink
line: For each entry in the top row of a 3×3, its row and column get crossed out, the leftover 2×2 slides out, and signs alternate.

source_title: Purplemath: Finding sequence patterns with common differences
title: Difference pyramid
line: Under 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 the differences 3, 5, 7, 9 appear, then 2, 2, 2, and the pyramid builds back up to 36.

source_title: Purplemath: What's a partial fraction? How does it decompose?
title: Two curves add to one
line: The graphs of 1/(x−1) and −1/(x+1) add point by point and land exactly on the graph of 2/(x²−1).

title: Cancel factors, not terms
line: The x's in (x+2)/(x+5) get wrongly crossed out, then plugging in x=1 gives 3/6 against 2/5, and the mistake flashes red.

source_title: Purplemath: Solving Exponential Equations from the Definition
title: Matching the bases
line: 4^(x+1)=8^x rewrites as 2^(2x+2)=2^(3x), the 2s fall away, and the graphs of both sides cross at x=2.

source_title: Purplemath: Solving Log Equations from the Definition
title: Unwrapping a log
line: log₂(x+3)=5 flips into 2⁵=x+3, and the curve y=log₂(x+3) meets the line y=5 at x=29.

title: The answer that isn't
line: Solving x/(x−2)=2/(x−2)+3 gives x=2, but the graphs show both sides blow up there, so the curves never actually meet.

source_title: Purplemath: Systems of Linear Equations: Definitions
title: Two lines, three outcomes
line: One line turns against a fixed line: they cross at one point, slide apart as parallels with none, then merge with infinitely many.

source_title: Purplemath: Graphing translated / transformed trig functions
title: Tuning a sine wave
line: Starting from y=sin x, A stretches it to height 3, B squeezes the period to π, C shifts it, D lifts it.

source_title: Purplemath: Working with angles of elevation and depression
title: Depression equals elevation
line: From a cliff, the angle looking down at a boat and the boat's angle looking up are shown to be alternate angles of equal size.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the sine, the cosine, and the tangent?
title: Ratios ignore size
line: A right triangle with a 35° angle grows and shrinks, its sides changing, while opposite over hypotenuse stays stuck at 0.574.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the sine, the cosine, and the tangent?
title: Whose opposite is it
line: The reference angle hops between the two acute corners of a right triangle, and the opposite and adjacent labels swap places.

source_title: Purplemath: How can trig identities help evaluate trig stuff?
title: sin 15° from 45 and 30
line: Angles of 45° and 30° on a unit circle leave a 15° gap, and sin(45°−30°)=(√6−√2)/4 matches the height of that point.

source_title: Purplemath: What are inverse trig ratios? What are they for?
title: Finding the angle from sides
line: A ray swings up from 0° and stops when its rise over run reaches 5/12, reading off the angle 22.6°.

source_title: Purplemath: What is an identity, and how do I prove it?
title: Work one side only
line: The left side tan x·cos x morphs step by step into sin x while the right side never moves, then their graphs overlap exactly.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Pythagorean Theorem? How does it work?
title: Four triangles rearranged
line: Four 3-4-5 triangles slide around inside a 7×7 square, first leaving a tilted 5×5 hole, then a 3×3 and a 4×4 hole.

source_title: Purplemath: What is the Pythagorean Theorem? How does it work?
title: Counting tiles
line: The 9 unit tiles on side 3 and the 16 on side 4 fly over and fill the 25-tile square on the hypotenuse.

source_title: Purplemath: Connecting geometric angles to algebra's x,y-plane
title: Triangles in every quadrant
line: A ray at 150° drops a line to the x-axis, making a 30° reference triangle with negative x; then 210° and 330° follow.

source_title: Purplemath: Converting between Radians and Degrees
title: Wrapping the radius
line: A radius peels off, bends around the circle, and fits a bit over 6 times, so a half turn is π radians or 180°.

source_title: Purplemath: Solving right-triangle word problems: Learn here!
title: How tall is the flagpole
line: From 20 m away at a 35° sight angle, a right triangle draws itself and 20×tan 35° counts up to a 14 m flagpole.

title: A slice of the whole
line: As a sector's angle sweeps to 360°, its area and arc length count up in step, ending at πr² and 2πr.

source_title: Purplemath: Solving trig equations is not as bad as it looks!
title: Every solution of sin x = 1/2
line: The line y=1/2 cuts a sine wave at π/6 and 5π/6, then again every 2π, matching two points on a unit circle beside it.

source_title: Purplemath: Special Angle Values: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 Triangles
title: Half a square, half a triangle
line: A unit square splits along its diagonal into a 1-1-√2 triangle, and an equilateral triangle of side 2 splits into 1, √3, 2.

source_title: Purplemath: Special Angle Values: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 Triangles
title: The square-root staircase
line: A point climbs a unit circle at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° while its height reads √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2.

source_title: Purplemath: Trigonometric Functions and Their Graphs: Sine and Cosine
title: Unrolling the circle
line: A point spins around a unit circle while its height is carried to the right, tracing out a sine wave one turn at a time.

source_title: Purplemath: Trigonometric Functions and Their Graphs: Sine and Cosine
title: Cosine is a shifted sine
line: The x-coordinate of a spinning point traces a cosine wave, which then slides right by π/2 and lands on the sine wave.

source_title: Purplemath: What are the basic trigonometric identities?
title: Building sin(A+B)
line: Two right triangles stack with angles A and B, and the top corner's height splits into sin A cos B plus cos A sin B.

title: Tangent on the circle
line: A ray from the center hits the line x=1 at height tan θ, which shoots up toward infinity as θ nears 90°.

title: Filling in the special points
line: The first quadrant's 30°, 45° and 60° points reflect across both axes, filling the circle with all sixteen special coordinates.
